<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but A's rebuttal work was more surgical. A repeatedly isolated real logical gaps in B's case: it showed that "not a perfect substitute" is not a concession of necessity, separated fragmentation (platform-splitting) from exclusion (price barriers) when B conflated them, and pressed B on the never-answered "meaningful share" threshold, which B's Rebuttal 2 answer (A4.1) dodged with a vague functional definition rather than any operational criterion — a real execution cost for B given A's pointed Q1. A also candidly conceded the symmetric evidentiary burden (A1 in Rebuttal 2) rather than dodging it, which read as honest rather than evasive. B's closing "irreversibility" framing was rhetorically the strongest moment of the debate, but A's closing directly answered it by flipping the asymmetry (lost development funding is also hard to recover), and B never fully engaged A's earlier "relative's TV / barbecue" counterexample showing accidental discovery isn't unique to paywalled finals. On balance A gave the cleaner, more disciplined path through the clash, while B's case, though vivid and emotionally resonant, left more live threads unaddressed by the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's [A4.3]/[A4.5] exchange — separating fragmentation from exclusion and turning B's own "accidental discovery" mechanism against the claim that only free finals enable it — did the most damage to B's unanswered threshold and discovery arguments, and B's closing reframe never fully repaired either gap.</best_rebuttal>
